analysis.one_liner: Requires police to get a judge-issued warrant before reading your stored emails.
analysis.headline: The Email Privacy Act, backed by senators from both parties, never got a vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the law written in 1986, the government can demand emails stored by a provider with a simple subpoena once messages are older than 180 days — no judge, no probable cause. This bill would require a search warrant from a judge before police or federal agents could force a provider to hand over the contents of anyone's stored emails, and it would let providers tell customers when the government asks for their records. It also lengthens how long courts can delay telling someone their records were taken, from 90 days to 180 days per order.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone who uses email, cloud storage, or messaging services. Today, prosecutors can compel providers to turn over stored emails with a subpoena — a document no judge reviews for probable cause. The bill would require a warrant based on probable cause, the same standard police need to search your desk drawers, and would generally let providers notify you when the government requests your data.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the old rules so the government can compel a provider to disclose the contents of stored emails or files only with a warrant issued under federal (or state) criminal procedures by a court of competent jurisdiction, instead of the lower bar that applied to older stored messages.
Lets providers notify a subscriber or customer that the government received a warrant, court order, subpoena, or request, unless a court grants an order delaying that notice.

Keeps narrower access for basic subscriber information (name, address, connection records, payment details), which can still be obtained by administrative or grand jury subpoena, so routine non-content data is not blocked.

analysis.who_pays: Law enforcement agencies lose the easy route to stored emails: they would have to persuade a judge there is probable cause, and prosecutors say warrant requirements add time and friction to investigations. The bill also extends the period courts can keep the person in the dark about a records demand from 90 to 180 days per order, which slightly weakens a privacy safeguard.

drawbacks.text: A warrant requirement slows investigators: under current law a prosecutor can get older stored emails with a prosecutor-issued subpoena, and this bill forecloses that path for content, which law enforcement argues can delay time-sensitive cases.

The bill lengthens the maximum duration of a delayed notification order to 180 days, renewable in further 180-day extensions, so someone under investigation could go well over a year without learning the government took their records.

The bill explicitly preserves the government's other surveillance tools — wiretap authorities, FISA, and congressional subpoenas — so it narrows one route to email content while leaving parallel routes intact.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but modest on the law-enforcement side: a judge reviewing a warrant application typically takes hours to days, and emergency exceptions remain in ordinary criminal procedure. Against that, the bill closes a loophole that lets police read years-old personal correspondence without any judicial finding of probable cause. The main honest criticism is the lengthened gag window — 180 days per order instead of 90 — which trades one privacy gain for a partial loss elsewhere.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee on day one, and the committee never took it up, so it died when the 115th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Lee introduced the Email Privacy Act in the Senate on July 27, 2017, joined by seven original cosponsors split between the parties (four Democrats, three Republicans).

The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; the action history shows no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no further action of any kind for the rest of the Congress.
Because Congress adjourned on January 3, 2019, the bill expired, and an identical bill would have to be reintroduced from scratch.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal and state investigators keep the status quo — the ability to compel stored emails with a subpoena and no judicial review — and the technology companies that process requests continue operating under the 1986 rules.

for.name: Sen. Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Email Privacy Act in the Senate on July 27, 2017.

for.name: Sens. Shaheen, Blumenthal, and Franken
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors, giving the bill bipartisan sponsorship from the start.

against.name: Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a committee markup or vote on the bill, which sat in committee from July 2017 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; it never received a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from the start — a Republican sponsor with four Democratic and three Republican cosponsors — so its death was not a partisan vote but a committee that never acted.

industries.note: Providers gain a single, clear rule — a warrant — instead of adjudicating a mix of subpoenas and court orders, and can notify customers about government demands. Companies like Google and Microsoft had publicly sought this update to the 1986 law because it reduces their legal uncertainty.

Agencies lose the ability to compel stored email content with an administrative or grand jury subpoena and must convince a judge of probable cause instead. What they give up is precisely the privacy the public gains.
